title: KPSS, the complementary test — and reading both together

explain.prompt: Explain to a colleague, in 5–7 sentences, why you run KPSS *in addition to* ADF. Use the four verdicts produced by the test code: TTF level, TTF returns, the persistent 2,000-observation series (conflict) and the 40-observation series (inconclusive). What do you do next in each of the two ambiguous cases?
rubric: KPSS reverses the null: H0 = stationary (around a level with 'c', a trend with 'ct'), H1 = unit root. Each test only protects its own H0, so crossing them prevents reading a non-rejection as a proof.
TTF level: ADF does not reject a unit root (p ≈ 0.91) and KPSS rejects stationarity (p ≤ 0.01) → concordant evidence of a unit root. Returns: the opposite → concordant evidence of stationarity.
Both reject (persistent series): neither a pure random walk nor simple stationarity — check the deterministic trend ('ct'), sub-periods for a break, changing variance, very long memory.
Neither rejects (40 obs): the data cannot decide — low power; rely on the economics of the series, the chart, and make the conclusions robust to both hypotheses.
statsmodels only tabulates KPSS p-values between 0.01 and 0.10: 0.01 means 'at most 0.01', 0.10 means 'at least 0.10' (InterpolationWarning).
Both tests must use the same deterministic specification; the trend-stationary series gives 'unit root' with 'c' and 'stationary' with 'ct'.
